Anterior shoulder dislocation: 5

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

An older patient has persistent inability to actively elevate the arm after a successfully reduced shoulder dislocation. Passive motion is substantially better, and imaging confirms reduction. Which associated soft-tissue injury should be investigated?

  1. Rotator cuff tear
  2. Bankart lesion
  3. Hill-Sachs lesion
  4. Reverse Hill-Sachs lesion
  5. Recurrent instability
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Rotator cuff tear

Persistent weakness after reduction, especially in older patients, warrants assessment for associated cuff injury.

Understanding the options

Rotator cuff tear
Persistent weakness after reduction, especially in older patients, warrants assessment for associated cuff injury.
Bankart lesion
A Bankart lesion involves the anteroinferior glenoid labrum, commonly after anterior dislocation. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Hill-Sachs lesion
An anterior dislocation may impact the posterolateral humeral head against the glenoid rim. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Reverse Hill-Sachs lesion
Posterior dislocation may cause an anteromedial humeral head impaction defect. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Recurrent instability
Capsulolabral injury can predispose to recurrent glenohumeral dislocation. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
